In my own constituency I can point to a market square that has not been resurfaced in thirty years, a bus interchange that floods every winter, and a former library building that has stood empty since 2013 while three separate community groups have asked to take it on. First, the bidding process must not reward the places with the most expensive consultants. Smaller district councils have lost a great deal of capacity over the last decade, and if the test is who can write the most polished prospectus, we will systematically funnel money towards authorities that already have the strongest hand. I would ask the Minister to confirm what capacity support will be made available to authorities in the lower priority categories. Secondly, the money must be additional. If it simply replaces revenue that has been withdrawn through other settlements, then we are recycling, not levelling up, and communities will notice. Thirdly, there must be a route for local people to shape the bids. The regeneration schemes that endure are the ones residents feel ownership of; the ones that fail are those imposed from a distance on the basis of a template. Finally, I would gently say that infrastructure alone will not do it. A refurbished high street with no bus after six o'clock, and no affordable childcare for the people who would work on it, is a photograph rather than a recovery. I support the fund. I want it to succeed, and I will keep pressing to make sure it does.

We should take that seriously, because a legislature that cannot recruit widely will eventually stop being able to govern well. There are practical things within our own control. We can improve the supports available to members with young families, which remain designed around a member whose spouse stays home. We can be far more rigorous about the harassment that staff in particular endure. We can extend the outreach programs that bring students into this building beyond the schools that happen to be within an easy bus ride of the capital. Ozara will grow up and choose her own path, and I hope it is flying rather than this. But I want the choice to be genuinely hers.

What we are witnessing in Syria is not a natural disaster. It is the predictable consequence of a set of political decisions taken by identifiable people, and the international community's response has too often been to treat it as weather: regrettable, vast, and nobody's fault. That framing suits everybody except the Syrian people. The humanitarian position is now desperate. The cross-border aid mechanism has been renewed only in truncated form, and each renewal has been used as leverage to extract concessions that have nothing to do with the delivery of food and medicine. Millions of people in the north-west depend on that single crossing. I would ask the Minister what contingency planning the Government has undertaken for the eventuality that the mechanism lapses altogether, and whether we are prepared to work through alternative routes even where that is politically uncomfortable. On accountability, I welcome the work of the international, impartial and independent mechanism, but the pace is glacial and the resourcing is thin. Evidence degrades. Witnesses die or become unreachable. If we are serious about the principle that the use of chemical weapons against civilians will be prosecuted, then we need to fund the bodies capable of prosecuting it, and we need to pursue universal jurisdiction cases in our own courts where the evidence supports them. Finally, on resettlement. We have taken a decision as a country about the numbers we will accept, and I understand the pressures behind it, but I would ask that Syrian cases that have been in the system for years now be resolved. Some of my own constituents have been waiting for family reunion decisions since 2019. That is not a policy; it is an administrative failure dressed up as one.

as somebody who has spent a good deal of time on buses in my own area, I want to say something about why bus reform matters more than almost anything else in that plan. Active travel is important and I support it, but for a great many of my constituents cycling to work is simply not realistic. They are working shifts that start before dawn, they are carrying tools, they live eight miles from the nearest employment site along a road with no footpath. For them, the bus is the only thing standing between them and a car they can barely afford to run. Over the last decade we have watched services in that position be withdrawn one by one, not because demand vanished but because the commercial model rewards frequency on profitable corridors and abandons everything else. Deregulation created a system in which the operator captures the profitable routes and the local authority is left to subsidise the remainder out of a budget that has shrunk every year. Franchising offers a way out of that, and I am glad the combined authority is looking at it seriously, but franchising is not free and it is not quick. It requires a funding settlement that lasts longer than one spending review, and it requires the authority to build up commissioning expertise it does not currently have. I would put two questions to the Minister. First, will the multi-year settlement that has been promised actually be multi-year, or will it be revisited at the next fiscal event? Operators will not invest in low-carbon fleet on the basis of a one-year commitment. Secondly, what is the Department's view on integrating fares across modes? A single ticket that works on bus, tram and rail would do more to shift behaviour than most of the capital projects we spend our time debating. The technology exists. What has been missing is the will to make operators share revenue.

I want to explain why I think that argument holds, and also to acknowledge honestly the objections to it, because they are not frivolous. The case for legislating is that testimony is finite. Within a decade there will be almost nobody left who can stand in a school hall and say: I was there, this happened to me, this is the number on my arm. When that generation is gone, the historical record becomes the only defence, and the historical record is precisely what deniers attack. They do not usually begin by saying it did not happen. They begin by quibbling over numbers, by insisting on impossible standards of documentary proof, by presenting themselves as brave dissenters against an official history. It is a technique, and it has been refined over sixty years. The objection, which I take seriously, is that criminalising a category of speech hands the denier the thing he most wants, which is martyrdom, and that the proper answer to bad history is better history. I have thought about this a great deal. My conclusion is that the two are not alternatives. Nothing in this law prevents us from funding education, from supporting museums, from sending every student to a site. We should do all of that and we should do more of it. But education operates on the assumption of good faith, and organised denial is not conducted in good faith. It is a political project with a political aim, and the aim is to make the murder of six million people arguable again. A society is entitled to say that some questions are settled. Not settled by government fiat, but settled by evidence so overwhelming that the pretence of doubt is itself a form of aggression. I will support the Bill, and I hope the House will do so with something close to unanimity.

My constituency is a rural one, and I want to speak briefly about the part of his life that resonates most strongly there. The Duke of Edinburgh's Award has, since 1956, taken young people out of classrooms and put them on hillsides with a map, a rucksack and each other. In Cumbria we have seen generations of them come through, often in weather that would test a mountain rescue team, and I have yet to meet anyone who completed a gold expedition and did not describe it as formative. What was radical about the scheme, and it was radical, was its premise: that character is developed by being given responsibility rather than by being lectured about it, and that this applies to every young person, not merely to those whose schools already offered such things. Millions have taken part across more than a hundred countries. That is a legacy of a very unusual kind, built patiently over sixty years without much interest in credit. He was also, long before it was fashionable, a serious voice on conservation. He understood that the natural world had a claim on us that was not reducible to what it could produce. Farmers in my constituency, who are not always warm towards people who lecture them about the environment, respected him because he knew what he was talking about and because he asked questions rather than issuing instructions. Above all, he made a choice in 1947 to subordinate a promising career of his own to a role with no job description and no precedent, and he sustained it for seventy-three years. On behalf of Penrith and The Border, I offer our condolences to Her Majesty and to the whole family.

It is not that non-indigenous young people are hostile. In my experience they are overwhelmingly not. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission gave us calls to action on education. They are not vague. They ask for age-appropriate curriculum on residential schools, treaties, and the historical and contemporary contributions of indigenous peoples, developed in consultation with survivors and indigenous educators, and mandatory rather than optional. Some provinces have moved. Others have produced a unit that appears in one grade and is dropped when a teacher runs short of time. We should be honest that a call to action which is implemented unevenly across thirteen jurisdictions is not implemented. I am not asking for federal intrusion into provincial curriculum, which would be both unconstitutional and counterproductive. I am asking the government to convene, to fund the development of materials that provinces can adopt, to support the training of indigenous teachers, and to report annually on progress in a form that allows this House to see where the gaps are. My son should not be the only child in the room who recognises the photograph.

question is not whether the measures announced yesterday are an improvement. They plainly are, and I give the Government credit for moving. The question is whether the scale of what has been announced matches the scale of what is coming, and on that I remain unconvinced. Let me set out why. The forecasts on which the announcement rests assume a return to trend growth within eighteen months. Every independent body I have read regards that as optimistic. If growth undershoots, the revenue does not appear, and the choice then becomes borrowing more, taxing more, or cutting again. It would be far better to have that conversation now, in advance, than to have it at three in the morning in a crisis. So my first request to the Government is for honesty about the contingency. What happens if the central forecast is wrong? Secondly, there is the question of who bears the cost. The measures announced are broadly flat in their distribution, which sounds fair until one remembers that the people at the bottom have no buffer at all. A household with savings can absorb a shock. A household that was already using a food bank in a good year cannot. The distributional analysis published alongside the statement stops at aggregate deciles and does not disaggregate by household type, and I would ask the Chancellor to publish the fuller analysis that I am confident his officials have prepared. Thirdly, capacity. Several of the announcements depend on delivery by local authorities and by an administrative system that has lost a great many experienced staff. Announcing a scheme is not the same as running one. I welcome the direction of travel. I simply say that the country has heard a great many announcements over the past two years, and what it now wants to see is money arriving in the right accounts, on time, without a helpline that nobody answers.

That is the point I would emphasise to colleagues who worry that we are proposing something unaffordable. We are not. We are proposing a reallocation, and the arithmetic is set out in the annex for anybody who wishes to check it. Let me deal with the objections we heard in evidence. The first is that any rebalancing creates losers, and that the losers will complain more loudly than the winners will cheer. That is true and it is why this has not been done, despite every government of the last twenty years acknowledging that the system is broken. Our answer is transition relief over a defined period, tapered, with certainty about the end point, so that businesses can plan. The second objection is that the valuation office lacks the capacity for more frequent revaluations. That is also true, and it is a resourcing decision rather than a law of nature. We recommend three-yearly revaluations moving to annual, with the necessary investment in the agency stated explicitly rather than buried. If the Government will not fund it, it should say so, and accept the consequence that valuations will continue to reflect a property market that no longer exists. The third objection is the most serious: that any property-based tax will always disadvantage businesses that need floorspace relative to those that do not. We accept that. It is why the report also recommends looking seriously at an online sales levy, and why we set out the design questions rather than pretending they are easy. What we resist is the argument that because the perfect answer is difficult, the current arrangement should continue indefinitely. It should not. It is actively hollowing out town centres, and we can see it happening.

They want to know whether the lorry that leaves on Tuesday will arrive on Wednesday, and whether the paperwork required will consume a person's entire working week. On that practical question, the Bill provides more clarity than the alternative, which is nothing. Let me be candid about the difficulties, because I do not think it serves anybody to pretend they are absent. There are genuine questions about how unfettered access operates in practice for goods that have been substantially transformed, and the definitions will need to be tested against real supply chains rather than model ones. There are questions about the treatment of goods at risk of onward movement, and about who bears the administrative cost of demonstrating that they are not at risk. Small firms cannot absorb that cost the way a large distributor can. And there are questions about the operation of the joint committee, which is where a great deal of the real decision-making will happen with very little visibility to this House or to the Assembly. I would ask the Minister for three things. First, a commitment to publish guidance for traders well in advance rather than in the final fortnight, which has been the pattern to date. Secondly, a dedicated support scheme for small and medium enterprises, funded properly, with people who answer the telephone. Thirdly, regular reporting to this House on the practical operation of the arrangements, including data on delays and rejected consignments. Certainty is not delivered by legislation alone. It is delivered when a haulier knows what will happen at the port. That is the test I will apply, and I suspect it is the only test that businesses in Northern Ireland will apply either.

At present a driver making a long journey may need four or five separate accounts, each with its own app, its own tariff structure and its own failure modes. Nobody accepts that at a petrol station. I would like to see enforceable uptime standards with a meaningful consequence for operators who fall short, and I would like the definition of uptime to exclude the trick of counting a unit as available when only one of its two sockets works. Third, and this is the one that matters most in a constituency like mine, there is the question of people without off-street parking. Roughly a third of households cannot charge at home, and for them the economics of electric ownership are entirely different. Public charging attracts the full rate of VAT while domestic electricity attracts five per cent. That is a regressive absurdity: the people least able to afford the vehicle pay the most to run it. The Treasury has been asked about this repeatedly and has given a holding answer each time. Finally, the grid. Local network capacity is now the binding constraint in several parts of my region, and distribution operators are quoting connection dates in the 2030s. No amount of consumer protection legislation will help if the electricity cannot physically get there.

It is a starting line that we should have crossed a decade ago, and I would remind the House that we signed in 2007. Ireland was among the last countries in Europe to ratify. That delay was not caused by drafting difficulties. It was caused by a decision to postpone until the domestic legal framework was aligned, and then by a failure to align it with any urgency. Now that we are ratifying, the question is what changes on Monday morning for a person with an intellectual disability living in a congregated setting in my constituency, or for a wheelchair user who cannot get on the train at their local station because there is nobody rostered to bring the ramp. My concerns are these. First, we are ratifying without the optional protocol. That means an individual whose rights under the convention are breached has no route to the committee once domestic remedies are exhausted. The Government has said it will consider the protocol after a period of implementation. I would ask the Minister to name a date, because open-ended consideration in this House has a way of lasting a very long time. Second, the deprivation of liberty provisions remain unresolved and the assisted decision-making legislation has still not been fully commenced. A convention that guarantees legal capacity sits very awkwardly with a wardship system we have not yet dismantled. Third, resourcing. Personal assistance hours have been effectively frozen while the population needing them has grown. Article 19 speaks about independent living. Independent living is delivered in hours of support, not in paragraphs. I welcome the motion, I will support it, and I intend to hold the Government to every article of what it is signing.

My constituents believe those two mandates cannot sit in one organisation, and having spent some time with the science, I agree with them. The numbers are stark. Returns on several Fraser runs have collapsed to a small fraction of historical averages. Some populations that supported communities for thousands of years are now measured in the hundreds of fish. This is happening across a species complex, in multiple watersheds, under multiple pressures, which is why single-cause explanations are unhelpful. Habitat loss, warming rivers, changes in ocean conditions, the cumulative effect of culverts and logging roads on spawning access, and yes, sea lice and pathogen transfer from net pens on migration routes all contribute. The petitioners are not asking the House to pretend that one factor explains everything. They are asking that the body assessing the risk from one of those factors not also be the body promoting it. Beyond the conflict of interest, my constituents ask for three things. They ask for the promised transition plan for open-net pens to be published with dates rather than aspirations, having now been delayed twice. They ask for habitat restoration funding to be delivered directly to the watershed roundtables and First Nations who are already doing the work, rather than routed through a grant process that consumes a year of volunteer time. And they ask for the science budget of the department to be protected, because we cannot manage what we have stopped measuring, and stock assessment capacity on the coast has been declining for two decades. I will table this petition with the certification, and I ask the minister to respond within the required period with something more substantial than a restatement of existing programs. The fish do not have another cycle to wait.

If a support exists and the intended beneficiaries are not taking it up, the answer is usually that the administrative burden exceeds the value, or that awareness is poor, and I have asked my officials to look at both. But it was framed as temporary and I do not intend to mislead anybody by suggesting otherwise. There is a further difficulty which the Deputy will appreciate. Excise reductions are passed through imperfectly. We have monitored forecourt prices and the pass-through has generally been reasonable, but it is not guaranteed, and every cent that is absorbed in margin rather than reflected at the pump is a cent of public money that has achieved nothing. That is an argument for targeted supports over blunt ones, and it is why I would rather put money into the fuel allowance and into direct payments to hauliers than into further general reductions. On the restoration path, I have said that it will be phased and I will give as much notice as I can. Businesses need to plan and I accept that a cliff edge would be damaging. But the House should understand that the current rates are below the minimum we are permitted to sustain indefinitely, and that constraint is not one I can set aside by ministerial preference.

The compliance yield in Scotland depends on decisions taken by an agency answerable to Ministers in another Parliament, with priorities set against a UK-wide picture in which Scotland is a rounding error. When Revenue Scotland took on the devolved taxes, it built a compliance function that costs a fraction of the equivalent per pound collected and achieves comparable or better results, precisely because it is small enough to know its taxpayer base. That is not a nationalist talking point; it is in the Auditor General's reports. On the specific measures before us, I want to raise the question of the registers. We have been promised a register of overseas entities for a decade. It has arrived, and it is welcome, but it is only as good as the verification behind it, and at present the verification is thin. A register that records whatever the applicant chooses to write is a directory, not a deterrent. Companies House reform helps, but the resourcing announced does not match the scale of the task, and I would ask the Minister to set out how many additional investigators will actually be in post by the end of the next financial year, as opposed to funded in principle. I would also press on enforcement against enablers. It is a recurring pattern that the structures we are trying to unwind were designed by professionals operating perfectly legally within our own jurisdiction, and that the regulatory response falls almost entirely on the client rather than on the adviser. Unexplained wealth orders were introduced with considerable fanfare and have been used a handful of times, largely because the costs risk of losing is prohibitive. Fix the costs regime and the tool becomes usable. Until then we are legislating for a power that agencies are too poor to exercise.

I mention this not to make a party point, though I am proud of it, but because it illustrates something about how the response to the pandemic worked in practice. Almost every effective intervention I saw was locally organised. The national schemes that worked were the ones that handed money and discretion to people who knew their area. The ones that struggled were designed centrally on the assumption that need is uniform, and then delivered through a contract awarded to an organisation with no presence on the ground. That is a lesson worth carrying forward, because we are going to need it. The immediate emergency has passed but the underlying picture in Cardiff, as in every city, is of households who entered the pandemic with nothing and have emerged with less than nothing. Debt has been the quiet story. Rent arrears, council tax arrears, buy-now-pay-later balances that do not appear on any credit file, and utility debt accumulating at a rate that the current support simply does not touch. The advice sector is seeing cases of a complexity they have not encountered before, and the funding for that sector is short-term and competitive, which means experienced advisers spend their winters writing bids. I would ask the Minister to look seriously at multi-year funding for advice services, because the return on that spending is well evidenced and immediate. I would also ask for a proper conversation about the interaction between reserved and devolved support. Households do not experience the constitutional settlement; they experience a payment arriving or not arriving. When the Welsh Government tops up a scheme and the top-up is treated as income for a reserved benefit, we have not helped anybody. We have simply moved money between two parts of the state while the family remains where it was.

It felt like an initiation into adult life, and I remember the manager coming out from behind the counter to shake my hand. Try getting that today. The reason I raise it is not nostalgia, although I confess to some. It is that the closure of branches has consequences that the banks consistently understate and that this House consistently underestimates. When the last branch in a town closes, the argument we are given is that footfall has declined and that customers have moved online. Both things are true and neither is the whole picture. Footfall declines partly because the hours have been cut to three mornings a week, and then the reduced footfall is cited as evidence of reduced demand. It is a managed decline with a self-justifying statistic attached. The people left behind are predictable: older customers, people with disabilities, those without reliable broadband, and small businesses that need to lodge cash. In my constituency there are farmers and shopkeepers who now drive forty minutes each way to lodge takings, and who are being told by their insurers that carrying that cash in a car is their own problem. The banking hub model has promise and I want it to work, but the rollout has been glacial and the criteria for triggering one are set in a way that excludes many of the places that need it most. I would ask the Minister three questions. What assessment has been made of the adequacy of the current access-to-cash framework in rural areas specifically? Will the Government legislate for a minimum service standard rather than relying on a voluntary agreement that the banks themselves negotiated? And what is being done about the resilience of the digital alternative, given that we have had significant outages this year during which entire towns could not transact at all? A cashless society is fine until the system is down.

the section 232 tariffs, the member knows as well as I do that the removal of those tariffs was not a concession we were given. It was negotiated, and it was negotiated in the face of a great deal of advice that it could not be done. Our aluminum producers in Quebec and British Columbia are today shipping into the American market without those duties, and I would invite the member to speak to the workers at those smelters about whether they regard that as a loss. On the specific question of the phase-in for the seventy per cent requirement, I want to explain the reasoning rather than simply assert that it is adequate. The requirement is meaningful only if the supply chain can actually meet it. If we had insisted on immediate application, the practical effect would have been that manufacturers sourced non-compliant material, paid the most-favoured-nation duty, and treated it as a cost of doing business. That helps nobody. Instead the phase-in gives our producers a defined runway during which they can secure the contracts, and it gives purchasers a clear signal about where they need to be. That is how content rules actually change behaviour. Now, the member raises the melt-and-pour question, and this is the legitimate part of his argument, so let me address it directly. It is true that the aluminum provisions do not include a melt-and-pour requirement of the kind that applies to steel, and it is true that this creates a theoretical route for offshore metal to be cast elsewhere and enter as compliant. We secured a commitment to review that question, with data collection beginning immediately so that the review is evidence-based rather than anecdotal. I would rather have a review grounded in trade flows we have actually measured than a rule we cannot enforce. We will monitor it, and if the data shows leakage, we will act on it.

The reason is straightforward and it is set out in the petition. Luton Council owns the airport. For years that ownership was held up, rightly, as a model of municipal enterprise: profits from the airport flowed directly into local services, funding youth provision, adult social care and voluntary sector grants to a level that neighbouring authorities could only envy. Then passenger numbers fell by ninety per cent in a matter of weeks, and a strength became a catastrophe. The council lost the great majority of its commercial income overnight, through no failure of management and no fault of the people of Luton. The consequence has been a savings programme of many millions of pounds, and the House should understand what that means in practice. It means the closure of libraries and community centres in some of the most deprived wards in the east of England. It means cuts to the very services that a town with high levels of child poverty and one of the youngest populations in the country most urgently requires. It means redundancies among staff who spent the previous year delivering food parcels and running test centres. The Government's response has been to point to the general support provided to local government and to the compensation scheme for lost sales, fees and charges. But that scheme explicitly excludes losses from commercial investments and from dividends of the kind Luton depends on. The council was doing precisely what successive governments told it to do, which was to reduce its reliance on grant by generating its own income, and it is now being penalised for having done so successfully. The petitioners therefore request that the House urge the Government to provide targeted support to Luton Council reflecting the particular circumstances of its airport ownership.

In February we were told in writing that no decision had been taken and that consultation with staff and service users would precede any change. In May, staff learned through a circular that the reconfiguration was proceeding. In September, following representations from myself and colleagues, we were told that the position had been misunderstood. Now we are told that it will not proceed in its entirety. Every one of those statements may be technically defensible. Together they have destroyed the confidence of a community in the process, and that lost confidence will make every future service change harder to deliver, including changes that are genuinely clinically justified. That is the real cost of doing this badly. Let me set out my substantive concern. The clinical case that has been advanced rests on volumes and on the recruitment difficulty in maintaining a rota. I accept that argument in principle. There are procedures that should be concentrated, and I would not ask any patient to accept a lower standard of care for the sake of geography. But the argument only holds if the receiving site actually has the capacity, and the receiving site in this instance is operating on trolleys most mornings of the week. Transferring activity into a hospital already in escalation is not centralisation; it is displacement. And the transport plan, such as it is, consists of a single line about ambulance capacity with no additional vehicles costed. I would ask the Minister for a written commitment on three points: that no service transfers before the receiving capacity is independently verified as in place; that the transport implications are costed and funded; and that whatever is finally decided is published in full, with the underlying clinical advice, so that people can see the reasoning rather than inferring it from rumour.

What we are discussing affects tens of thousands of families and it is being taken at a time when the Chamber is nearly empty and when there is no realistic prospect of a decision following from it. I say that not to score a point against the Minister of State, who has always been courteous in dealing with me, but because the scheduling of business is itself a statement of priority, and the message being sent is unmistakable. Let me turn to the substance. The core of the problem is that we have a policy which is admirable on paper and an implementation system which is not resourced to deliver it. Every review of this area for the past fifteen years has reached the same conclusion, and each time the response has been a new strategy rather than staff. Strategies are cheap. A strategy can be launched with a photograph and a document and it costs nothing until somebody has to do the work. Staff cost money, they take years to train, and they do not produce an announcement. That asymmetry explains a great deal about how this State makes decisions. I want to give the House one specific example from my own constituency. A family contacted me in March about an assessment that had been due since the previous year. They have poured billions of dollars of new spending into an economy that was already running hot, and then expressed astonishment when the price level responded. Now, I want to be careful here, because the government's defenders will say, correctly, that inflation is a global phenomenon, that supply chains were disrupted everywhere, and that energy prices moved for reasons that have nothing to do with any Canadian policy decision. All of that is true. It is also incomplete. The question is not whether global factors exist; it is whether domestic decisions made the domestic outcome worse than it needed to be. And on that question, the government's own budget documents provide the answer. Spending that was announced as emergency, temporary and targeted has become permanent, general and untargeted. Programs introduced with a stated end date have been extended three times. The fiscal anchor has been redefined twice, which is what one does when the anchor is inconvenient. The consequence falls hardest on exactly the people the government claims to be helping. Inflation is the most regressive tax there is. A family with assets sees the nominal value of those assets rise. A family that rents, and spends most of its income on food and fuel, simply becomes poorer, and there is no exemption to apply for. In my riding I have food banks reporting demand from people who are employed full time. That is a new phenomenon and it should alarm everybody in this chamber. What would I do differently? Return to a credible fiscal anchor and state it publicly. Subject every new program to a test of whether it adds to demand or to supply, and favour the latter. And address the supply side of housing, which is where the price pressure is most acute and where federal spending has so far succeeded mainly in bidding up the price of the existing stock.

I raise that counterfactual not to indulge in speculation for its own sake but because it bears directly on the argument being made about the powers we are discussing. The case for retaining them rests on the proposition that they will only ever be used by people of sound judgement in circumstances of obvious necessity. History does not support that confidence. It is precisely the point of constitutional constraint that it operates when judgement fails, and the people who design constraints must assume that at some point the wrong person will hold the office. That is not a slur on any current holder. It is the ordinary logic of institutional design, and we apply it everywhere else without embarrassment. We do not permit a chief constable to authorise their own surveillance on the grounds that chief constables are generally decent people. Now, the counter-argument, which I want to address fairly, is that flexibility has served this country well. Our constitutional arrangements are uncodified, they have adapted to circumstances that a written text could not have anticipated, and the absence of rigid rules allowed decisions in 1940 that a more constrained system might have prevented. There is something in that. My answer is that the flexibility which allowed Churchill to be installed was not the absence of rules; it was the presence of a convention, well understood, that a Prime Minister who has lost the confidence of the House goes. Conventions are constraints. They are simply constraints that depend on shared understanding rather than on enforcement, and shared understanding is exactly what has been eroding. When a convention is broken and nothing happens, it stops being a convention. That is the process we are living through, and this Bill either arrests it or accelerates it.

We currently make commitments that bind future taxpayers who have no say in them, and we do so with almost no formal mechanism for representing their interest. Consider infrastructure, where we routinely choose the cheaper option at construction and impose a maintenance liability on people who will be born after the decision is taken. Consider pensions, where the intergenerational transfer is explicit and where we have repeatedly chosen to protect current recipients at the expense of future ones because current recipients vote. None of that is corruption or incompetence. It is the ordinary operation of a system in which the affected party is absent from the room. There are institutional answers to this. Wales legislated for a future generations commissioner with statutory powers to require public bodies to demonstrate how their decisions serve long-term wellbeing, and while the evidence on its effectiveness is mixed, the mechanism is instructive: it does not give anybody a veto, it forces a justification onto the record. Finland runs a parliamentary committee for the future which reviews government policy against long-horizon scenarios. Neither model has transformed its country. Both have changed what officials are required to think about before they write advice, which over time is not nothing. What I would propose here is modest. Every significant policy proposal coming before this House should carry an assessment of its effects at twenty and fifty years, prepared independently, and published. Where the effects cannot be estimated, that should be stated. It would slow nothing down and it would make visible a category of consequence that at present we simply do not discuss. The objection will be that it becomes a box-ticking exercise. That is a risk with any procedural requirement. The answer is to make the assessments public and let others hold us to them, which is how environmental impact assessment eventually acquired teeth.

again. This year I want to speak about something slightly different, which is the machinery of it rather than the horror of it. We tend to discuss the Holocaust as an eruption of evil, and understandably so, because the scale of it resists any other language. But the more I have read, and the more survivors I have listened to, the more I have come to think that the truly frightening thing is how ordinary the administration of it was. The deportations required timetables. Somebody scheduled the trains and somebody costed the fares, and the fares were charged to the deportees. Registers were maintained. Property was inventoried and sold at auction, and the receipts were filed. The people doing that work were clerks, accountants, station managers, lawyers who drafted the decrees that removed citizenship, doctors who signed certificates. Very few of them were fanatics. Most of them were doing their jobs within a system that had, step by step, redefined a category of person as outside the scope of ordinary obligation. That is what I think we owe the memory of the victims: not only grief, but attention to the process. Because the process is repeatable, and the early stages of it are not dramatic. They consist of language that reclassifies people, of exemptions from rules that were supposed to be universal, of officials being told that a particular category of case does not require the usual safeguards. Anybody who has worked in government will recognise how easily that can happen without anybody intending it. So when we say never again, I would suggest that the vigilance required is not primarily against people in uniform shouting slogans. It is against the quiet administrative moment when someone in an office decides that the ordinary rules do not apply to this group, and nobody in the room objects, because objecting would be awkward.

The vaccination programme is working, but it is working with a lag. A dose given today confers protection in two to three weeks. Let me explain why I think bilateral commitments of this kind are more valuable than another round of headline targets. The multilateral process has produced ambition. vaccination and testing, and yet the tests themselves have been treated as an afterthought at every stage of this. I want to lay out the sequence, because the pattern is instructive. In the spring, we were told that antigen tests were unreliable and that their use would create false reassurance. In the summer, we were told that they had a role in specific settings. In the autumn, they were recommended for close contacts in schools. Now they are being distributed, in insufficient quantities, at a price that puts a family's weekly testing beyond the means of the households most likely to be exposed. Each of those positions was defended at the time as following the evidence. The evidence did not change that much. What changed was the availability, and I think we would have more public confidence today if that had simply been said at the outset. On the substance, the argument against antigen tests always rested on sensitivity relative to PCR, which is a real limitation and which nobody disputes. But that comparison answers the wrong question. The relevant question is not whether an antigen test is as sensitive as a PCR test. It is whether a test that can be taken at home, twice a week, with a result in fifteen minutes, detects more infectious people in a population than a test that is more sensitive but which requires an appointment, a journey, and a two-day wait during which the person continues their normal activities. Frequency beats sensitivity for transmission control, and that has been in the literature for eighteen months. My asks are simple. Make the tests free at the point of use, as several of our neighbours have done. Distribute them through schools, workplaces and pharmacies without a requirement to register. And build a reporting mechanism that is voluntary and simple, so that we actually learn something from the millions of tests being taken.

Lady's substantive point about capacity, I agree entirely and I would add one observation. The absence she describes is not a shortage of good people. Every difficult question is escalated because no one below the political level is empowered to settle it, and the political level is consumed with other matters. We discovered, in real time and at considerable cost, that we did not know which facilities were single points of failure, we did not know the inventory position of critical goods, and we did not know which of our corridors could absorb a diversion. Other countries did know, because they had done the mapping. Let me be specific about what I mean, because supply chain mapping is a phrase that can mean almost anything. I mean an inventory of the physical assets: the ports and their berth capacity, the rail interchanges and their throughput, the highway corridors and their bridge weight restrictions, the cold storage capacity by region, the fuel distribution network. I mean the flows across them, by commodity, at a level of granularity that lets you model what happens when one node fails. And I mean the governance question: who has the authority to reroute, and how quickly, when a node does fail. At present the answer to that last question is that authority is distributed across two levels of government, several agencies, and a large number of private operators whose commercial interests do not align with each other during a disruption. During the western floods, the actual coordination happened through a series of telephone calls between people who happened to know each other. That is not a system. It worked because of individual competence, and we should not build a national economy on the hope that the right individuals are on shift. The task force that was announced has produced recommendations. I have read them. They are sensible and they are unfunded, and the implementation report that was promised has not appeared. The obvious answer, which every comparable country has arrived at, is to use the counter for services that require identity verification and a human being: banking for those without a branch, government identity services, licence renewals, payment of local charges, and services on behalf of utilities. Some of that has been done here, in pieces, without a strategy. In France and in Italy the postal network is a substantial financial institution. In the UK the banking framework agreement gives customers of every major bank access at the counter. We have made progress on the offline services agreement and I welcome it, but it remains far short of what is possible, and each Department negotiates separately, which means the network is dealing with a dozen counterparties who each want a discount. What I would ask the Minister for is a whole-of-government decision: that where a service can be delivered at a post office counter, it is offered there by default, with a single agreement covering the sector. That is a decision that costs the Exchequer nothing net, because the transaction has to happen somewhere, and it would transform the viability of the network overnight.

I want to be careful here, because that argument is frequently made in bad faith, and I do not want to be understood as making it. The lesson of that episode is not that indigenous communities cannot manage money. It is that any organization, anywhere, handed a large sum on short notice with a spending deadline and no institutional infrastructure will spend it badly, and that we knew this and did it anyway. The federal government designed those conditions. We attached the deadline, we structured it as a one-time transfer rather than as sustained funding, and we provided no support for the procurement and project management capacity that a build of that scale requires. Then we expressed surprise. So what I would propose is different in three respects. First, funding should be predictable and multi-year, so that a community can hire a qualified project manager on a permanent basis rather than contracting one at a premium for a single build. Second, the capacity support should be funded separately and should be genuinely at the community's direction, rather than being a consultant selected by the department. Third, the accountability should run to the community members first. The current reporting burden is extraordinary, running to dozens of reports annually to multiple departments, and almost none of it is directed to the people actually served. Reverse that. Fund an independent audit function that reports to the membership. That is what accountability means everywhere else in this country, and there is no reason it should mean something different here.

I want to use my time to talk about the gap between what we have committed to and what we are actually doing, because I think that gap is now the central problem rather than the level of ambition. Our targets are, on paper, among the more ambitious in Europe. The carbon budgets have been adopted. The sectoral ceilings have been agreed after a long and difficult negotiation. A target is adopted by a Government; the reductions are delivered by hundreds of thousands of individual decisions about what vehicle to buy, what heating system to install, what to do with a field. Those decisions respond to prices, to available alternatives, and to what is administratively possible, and we have not changed any of those enough. Take retrofit. The grant scheme is generous by historical standards and the uptake is below target, because the up-front contribution is beyond most households, because the contractor capacity does not exist, and because the process requires a level of project management that a working family cannot supply. Fixing that requires a one-stop delivery model with financing attached to the property rather than the person, which has been recommended repeatedly. Take agriculture, which is the difficult conversation nobody in this House wants to have honestly. The ceiling agreed will not be met by efficiency measures alone. It will require a change in output, and that means income support for a transition that farmers did not ask for. Saying so is not anti-farmer. Pretending otherwise is.

I mention that because the debate about the Defence Forces in this House tends to be conducted at the level of policy abstraction, and the reality in a garrison town is quite different and rather more concrete. It is families, schools, local businesses, and a set of relationships built over generations. When we discuss establishment numbers, we are discussing whether those things continue. The exit data tells us why with complete clarity: pay, working conditions, the absence of a proper mechanism for representation, and the accumulated effect of being asked to do more with less over a long period. Every one of those is within our power to change and each of them has been the subject of a report. The pay issue is the most straightforward and I would urge the Minister not to be deflected by comparisons with other public service grades. The relevant comparison is not with a civil servant; it is with what a qualified technician, having been trained at public expense, can earn in the private sector six months after leaving. We are currently operating, in effect, a publicly funded apprenticeship scheme for private employers. On working conditions, the accommodation in several barracks is not acceptable and has not been for years. A designation without a management plan is a line on a chart. Second, the resourcing of enforcement. We have a very large maritime area, among the largest in Europe relative to our landmass, and the assets available to patrol it are limited and are frequently tied up alongside for want of crew. Whatever regime we design, it will be enforced by people in boats, and there are not enough of them. Third, and this is where the fishers' objection has real force, the consultation process. The inshore fleet is composed of small operators who cannot take a day off the water to attend a hearing in Dublin, who do not have legal representation, and who are asked to respond to documents running to hundreds of pages within a statutory period designed for institutional consultees. Their exclusion is structural rather than deliberate, but the effect is the same, and it means that the people with the most detailed knowledge of the areas being planned are the least represented in planning them. I would ask the Minister to commit to a dedicated inshore consultation process with support for participation.

What unites those situations is that nobody arrives at a hospital by choice, and that the person arriving is, almost by definition, not at their best. That is the context in which we should evaluate the practice of charging for the car park. The defence offered is that charging manages demand, prevents the site being used by shoppers and commuters, and generates revenue that goes back into services. Let me take those in turn. Demand management is a real consideration and it can be addressed by validation: a barrier that reads a code issued at reception. That is a solved problem, technologically, and it is used in other countries. The abuse argument therefore justifies a control mechanism, not a charge. On revenue, the sums involved are not trivial for a hospital trust and I do not want to pretend otherwise. But we should be honest about what the revenue is. It is a charge levied on the sick and their families, collected at the moment of maximum distress, and it falls hardest on those attending most frequently, which means people with chronic conditions, people on dialysis, and parents of children with complex needs. A family in my constituency with a child in long-term treatment calculated their parking costs at more than two thousand pounds over eighteen months. There is a discretionary concession scheme; it requires an application, most people do not know it exists, and the staff who could tell them are busy. Then there is the enforcement, which is where most of my casework arises. Contracts are let to private operators paid through the penalties they issue, which produces exactly the behaviour one would predict: charges issued to people whose appointment overran, and appeals processes designed to be abandoned. That incentive structure should not exist on an NHS site.

But I want to press on the question of what follows the statement, because a declaration without consequence eventually becomes a form of absolution: we have said the thing, we have discharged the obligation, and the trade continues. There is now substantial evidence that goods entering this country are produced with forced labour in the region concerned, and the current legal framework requires only that a company publish a statement about what it has done. A statement is not a duty. Other jurisdictions have moved to a rebuttable presumption, whereby goods from the region are excluded unless the importer can demonstrate otherwise, and the effect has been immediate because the burden sits with the party that has the information. Will the Government adopt that model, and if not, why not? Second, on the procurement of our own public bodies. It has been established that equipment purchased by public authorities in this country originates with entities directly implicated. We control that entirely. It requires no international agreement and no negotiation. Third, on the position of those who have sought refuge here. Members of the community in the UK have reported surveillance and pressure on relatives at home, and the response of the police has been inconsistent because the offences involved sit awkwardly across several statutes. I would ask what guidance has been issued. Finally, a word about the strategic argument, which is always made in these debates: that raising these matters costs us commercially and diplomatically. I want to put that contrast at the centre of what I have to say, because it is not an accident of administration. It reflects a set of choices about who the state is built to serve. The resiliency point is the deeper one. We have known for forty years that an economy dependent on commodity extraction experiences a cycle, that the cycle is driven by prices set elsewhere, and that the way out is to use the revenue from the good years to build something that survives the bad ones. Norway did that and has a fund of extraordinary size. We did not. We spent the revenue, we cut the taxes, and now, in the downturn, we are told there is no fiscal room. That is not bad luck. It is the predictable result of a decision taken repeatedly across governments of every stripe, including some that I have supported. What would diversification actually look like? It means processing here rather than shipping raw product for others to add value to. It means a serious industrial strategy for the sectors adjacent to what we already do well: engineering, environmental remediation, advanced manufacturing, all of which employ the same skills. It means training funded at a scale that lets a forty-five-year-old with a family retrain without losing their house, which the current programs do not remotely permit. And it means public investment in the transition rather than waiting for a market signal that arrives, if at all, after the community has emptied out. The alternative is what we are watching now: a downturn managed through unemployment insurance and out-migration, with the young leaving first, and a recovery that arrives too late for the towns that needed it most.

That is the entire function of the backstop and it is the point that gets lost in the noise. It is not a preferred outcome. Nobody in this House wants it to be operative. It is an insurance policy, and an insurance policy that lapses when the other party finds it inconvenient is not insurance at all. I want to address the objection directly, because it is made sincerely by people I respect. The objection is that a mechanism with no time limit is not a backstop but a permanent arrangement imposed without consent, and that no sovereign state should accept an obligation from which it cannot unilaterally withdraw. I understand the force of that. My response is that the alternative on offer is an assurance about future intentions, and that the situation on this island is precisely one in which assurances about future intentions have been found insufficient by everybody who has had to live with the consequences. The Border is not an abstraction to the people who live along it. It runs through farms, through parishes, and in places through individual buildings. There are hundreds of crossings. It cannot be policed and everybody who has studied it knows it cannot be policed. What can happen is that infrastructure appears at a small number of crossings and becomes a target, and then the response to the target becomes further infrastructure, and we know exactly where that sequence goes because we lived it for thirty years. So when I say to the Taoiseach that we cannot wish a border away, I mean that the choice is between a mechanism that keeps it invisible and a process that makes it visible again by increments, with each increment individually defensible and the cumulative outcome one nobody chose.

the claim that they are the ones actually being silenced. It is a remarkably effective move and I want to spend a moment taking it apart, because it recurs in every context where these arguments are made and it is not always recognised for what it is. The structure of the argument runs as follows. A person makes a statement that is demonstrably false and that causes identifiable harm to an identifiable group. The statement is contradicted, publicly, with evidence. The person then declares that the contradiction is censorship, that they are being persecuted for asking questions, and that the vigour of the response proves they have touched something the establishment wishes to conceal. Every element of the response is thereby converted into confirmation. Disagreement becomes evidence. Silence would also be evidence. There is no possible reaction that does not feed the claim, which is precisely why the move is chosen. What makes it work is that it borrows the language of a genuine and important principle. Free expression matters, dissent matters, and there are real cases of people penalised for holding unpopular but honestly held views. Those cases exist and we should defend them. The borrowing is deliberate: by dressing an assertion of falsehood in the clothing of dissent, they invite decent people who care about liberty to defend them on principle without examining what is actually being said. And a good many decent people accept the invitation. So what is the answer? Not, I think, prohibition in most cases, which supplies the martyrdom the argument requires. The answer is to insist on the distinction between the right to say a thing and the entitlement to have it treated as credible. Nobody is owed an audience, a platform, or the presumption that their claim is arguable. Refusing to grant those is not censorship. It is judgement, and a society that cannot exercise judgement will be governed by whoever shouts.
